items.stem: What is science?

options.label: A
options.text: A method of memorizing facts and figures about the universe

options.label: B
options.text: A process of conducting experiments without any specific questions

options.label: C
options.text: A way of thinking, observing, and doing things to understand the world

options.label: D
options.text: A collection of beliefs about how things work

items.answer: (C) A way of thinking, observing, and doing things to understand the world. Science is a systematic approach involving curiosity, questioning, exploration, and experimentation to understand the natural world and the universe. It is a dynamic process of discovery rather than a static set of facts.

items.stem: Why is science described as a “giant and unending jigsaw puzzle”?

options.label: A
options.text: Because it is a game that only a few can play

options.label: B
options.text: Because new discoveries add pieces, leading to more questions

options.label: C
options.text: Because it has a fixed number of pieces to be discovered

options.label: D
options.text: Because it is primarily about solving complex mathematical problems

items.answer: (B) Because new discoveries add pieces, leading to more questions. Science is likened to an unending jigsaw puzzle because each new finding or discovery provides a piece of understanding, which in turn opens up new questions and areas for further exploration, making the process continuous.

items.stem: What is the scientific method?

options.label: A
options.text: A rigid set of rules that must be followed in a specific order

options.label: B
options.text: A way to prove pre-existing beliefs about the natural world

options.label: C
options.text: A step-by-step process of observing, questioning, guessing, and testing

options.label: D
options.text: A method used exclusively by professional scientists in laboratories

items.answer: (C) A step-by-step process of observing, questioning, guessing, and testing. The scientific method is a systematic approach to investigation that involves making observations, formulating questions, making educated guesses (hypotheses), and then testing these guesses through experiments or further observations to arrive at conclusions.

items.stem: A student notices that plants kept in a dark room do not grow well. Using the scientific method, what would be their next logical step after this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately conclude that all plants need sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: Ask a question, such as “Does sunlight affect plant growth?”

options.label: C
options.text: Conduct an experiment by giving some plants extra fertilizer

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore the observation as it might be a coincidence

items.answer: (B) Ask a question, such as “Does sunlight affect plant growth?” After making an observation (plants in a dark room not growing well), the next step in the scientific method is to formulate a question based on that observation to guide further investigation.

items.stem: Why is it said that anyone using the scientific method is acting like a scientist?

options.label: A
options.text: Because only professional scientists use the scientific method

options.label: B
options.text: Because the scientific method is about common sense, which everyone possesses

options.label: C
options.text: Because everyday problem-solving often involves observing, guessing, and testing

options.label: D
options.text: Because scientists are the only ones who ask questions about the world

items.answer: (C) Because everyday problem-solving often involves observing, guessing, and testing. The basic principles of the scientific method—like observing, asking questions, forming hypotheses, and testing them—are often used in everyday situations, such as finding out why a pen has stopped working or why food spilled from a cooker.

items.stem: How is science different from just memorizing facts?

options.label: A
options.text: Memorizing facts is more important in science than the process of discovery

options.label: B
options.text: Science is a dynamic process of inquiry, while memorizing is passive

options.label: C
options.text: True science does not involve any memorization of facts at all

options.label: D
options.text: Memorizing facts is the first step of the scientific method

items.answer: (B) Science is a dynamic process of inquiry, while memorizing is passive. Science involves actively thinking, observing, and experimenting to understand how things work, rather than simply memorizing facts and figures.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a step in the scientific method?

options.label: A
options.text: Observing something that is interesting

options.label: B
options.text: Guessing a possible answer to a question

options.label: C
options.text: Accepting a guess without testing it

options.label: D
options.text: Testing a guess through experiments or more observations

items.answer: (C) Accepting a guess without testing it. The scientific method involves testing guesses (hypotheses) through experiments or further observations. Accepting a guess without any form of testing goes against the principles of scientific inquiry.

items.stem: Imagine you are trying to figure out why your flashlight isn’t working. First, you observe it’s not turning on. You guess the batteries might be dead. You then replace the batteries. According to the scientific method described, what is your action of replacing the batteries an example of?

options.label: A
options.text: Making an initial observation

options.label: B
options.text: Forming a question

options.label: C
options.text: Testing your guess (hypothesis)

options.label: D
options.text: Analyzing the results

items.answer: (C) Testing your guess (hypothesis). In this scenario, observing the flashlight not working is the initial observation. Guessing the batteries are dead is forming a hypothesis. The act of replacing the batteries is the step of testing that hypothesis to see if it resolves the problem.

items.stem: What does the idea that “new discoveries often change our understanding of the world” suggest about scientific knowledge?

options.label: A
options.text: Scientific knowledge is absolute and never changes

options.label: B
options.text: Scientific knowledge can evolve and be revised based on new evidence

options.label: C
options.text: Old scientific discoveries are always incorrect and should be discarded

options.label: D
options.text: Understanding the world is not possible through science

items.answer: (B) Scientific knowledge can evolve and be revised based on new evidence. This statement highlights that science is a progressive field. As new evidence emerges and new discoveries are made, existing scientific understanding can be refined, modified, or even overturned, reflecting the dynamic nature of scientific knowledge.

items.stem: What is a key benefit of working together with friends in science?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes experiments less accurate

options.label: B
options.text: It is always more fun to discover things together

options.label: C
options.text: It helps in memorizing facts more easily

options.label: D
options.text: It eliminates the need for individual curiosity

items.answer: (B) It is always more fun to discover things together. Collaborative learning in science makes discovery more enjoyable, and reflects how scientists often work together in teams to solve problems and share ideas.

items.stem: What is the term for a guess or a possible answer to a scientific question before it is tested?

options.label: A
options.text: A theory

options.label: B
options.text: A law

options.label: C
options.text: A hypothesis

options.label: D
options.text: An observation

items.answer: (C) A hypothesis In the scientific method, a hypothesis is an educated guess or a proposed explanation for an observation, which is then tested through experimentation or further observation to determine its validity.

items.stem: What does the phrase “To be a wise person, you must be a ‘whys’ person!” emphasize about learning science?

options.label: A
options.text: Memorizing answers to all “why” questions

options.label: B
options.text: Constantly asking questions and seeking understanding

options.label: C
options.text: Believing everything you are told without questioning

options.label: D
options.text: Avoiding difficult questions in science

items.answer: (B) Constantly asking questions and seeking understanding. This phrase encourages a curious and inquisitive mindset, highlighting that the path to wisdom and scientific understanding involves consistently asking “why” and seeking deeper explanations for phenomena observed in the world.

items.stem: If a student observes that a particular type of bird is only seen during winter in their area, what scientific question could arise from this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Are all birds migratory?

options.label: B
options.text: Why does this bird species appear only in winter?

options.label: C
options.text: What is the bird’s favorite food?

options.label: D
options.text: How many feathers does this bird have?

items.answer: (B) Why does this bird species appear only in winter? The observation of a bird appearing seasonally would naturally lead to a question about the reason for this specific pattern, such as investigating its migratory behavior or seasonal adaptations.

items.stem: Where can science be found in our daily lives?

options.label: A
options.text: Only in laboratories and research institutions

options.label: B
options.text: Only in textbooks and scientific journals

options.label: C
options.text: Everywhere, from the depths of the ocean to outer space

options.label: D
options.text: Only in complex natural phenomena, not everyday things

items.answer: (C) Everywhere, from the depths of the ocean to outer space. The explicitly states that “the most wonderful thing about science is that it is everywhere,” encompassing a vast range of scales and environments, from the microscopic to the cosmic, and including everyday occurrences.

items.stem: What does the idea of moving a puzzle piece in science refer to?

options.label: A
options.text: The idea that scientific experiments often fail

options.label: B
options.text: The self-correcting nature of science where existing ideas are revised with new evidence

options.label: C
options.text: The fact that scientists often misplace their equipment

options.label: D
options.text: The process of creating new scientific theories from scratch

items.answer: (B) The self-correcting nature of science where existing ideas are revised with new evidence. This analogy refers to the way scientific understanding evolves. When new data or better explanations emerge, previously accepted ideas or theories might be re-evaluated and modified, demonstrating science’s capacity to correct and refine itself.

items.stem: What is the primary aim of asking questions and exploring the world in science?

options.label: A
options.text: To prove personal opinions

options.label: B
options.text: To understand how things work and uncover secrets of the universe

options.label: C
options.text: To create complex technologies immediately

options.label: D
options.text: To find the simplest answers to all questions

items.answer: (B) To understand how things work and uncover secrets of the universe. Science is the pursuit of understanding how the world and the universe work, involving exploration, asking questions and discovering the principles of nature..

items.stem: The example of a bicycle repair person trying to find an air leak is used to illustrate:

options.label: A
options.text: That only mechanics use the scientific method

options.label: B
options.text: How complex scientific problems are solved

options.label: C
options.text: That everyday problem-solving can involve a scientific approach

options.label: D
options.text: The importance of having the right tools for science

items.answer: (C) That everyday problem-solving can involve a scientific approach. This example, along with others like a cook figuring out why dal spilled, is used to show that the systematic process of questioning, guessing, and testing (the scientific method) is not limited to formal science but is also applied in everyday problem-solving scenarios.

items.stem: What is the new subject introduced for exploring the world in the Middle Stage of school?
items.answer: Science

items.stem: What is the most important quality needed for science?
items.answer: Curiosity.

items.stem: What is the title of the Grade 6 Science textbook mentioned?
items.answer: Curiosity.

items.stem: Name one mystery of nature that science helps unravel.
items.answer: Why stars shine.

items.stem: Where can science be found, according to the text?
items.answer: Everywhere.

items.stem: Do new scientific discoveries ever lead to changes in our understanding?
items.answer: Yes

items.stem: Which planet is uniquely known to support life?
items.answer: Earth.

items.stem: Besides food, what essential substance do we need for survival mentioned in the text?
items.answer: Water.

items.stem: What happens to water when it is cooled sufficiently?
items.answer: It freezes and becomes ice.

items.stem: What is produced when water is heated sufficiently?
items.answer: It boils and becomes steam.

items.stem: What everyday object was used as an example for applying the scientific method when it stops working?
items.answer: A pen.

items.stem: What is the first step in the scientific method after observing something?
items.answer: Wonder and think of a question.

items.stem: What are people called who follow the scientific method to solve problems?
items.answer: Scientists

items.stem: Can a person be considered working like a scientist if they follow the scientific method in daily life?
items.answer: Yes.

items.stem: What is the foremost thing needed to learn science well?
items.answer: To be curious and observe surroundings keenly.

items.stem: When curiosity is sparked, what kinds of questions do we begin to ask?
items.answer: How and why.

items.stem: Is science typically an individual or a team effort?
items.answer: A team effort.

items.stem: What kind of “person” should you be to become a wise person?
items.answer: A “whys” person.

items.stem: Explain the meaning of “Science” .
items.answer: Science is a way of thinking, observing, and doing things to understand our world and uncover the universe’s secrets, like a grand adventure of inquiry.

items.stem: Why is the Grade 6 Science textbook titled “Curiosity”?
items.answer: The textbook is titled “Curiosity” because having curiosity is the most important thing needed to explore, ask questions, and understand how things work in science.

items.stem: List two examples of natural phenomena that suggests science helps us understand.
items.answer: Science helps us understand mysteries like why stars shine in the night sky and how a flower knows the precise moment to bloom.

items.stem: What interesting aspect of food in India does the chapter point out?
items.answer: The chapter points out that in a diverse country like India, food is fascinating, with different cuisines and many tasty dishes to explore.

items.stem: What are two questions about water that the chapter encourages readers to think about?
items.answer: The chapter encourages readers to wonder why and how it rains, and to notice how water changes form when cooled or heated.

items.stem: Name three different types of materials mentioned in the chapter that we use.
items.answer: The chapter mentions materials such as paper we write on, a metal key, a plastic ruler, a rubber eraser, magnets, and clothes.

items.stem: How does the chapter suggest we can expand our scientific inquiry beyond Earth?
items.answer: The chapter suggests expanding our inquiry by asking questions about celestial bodies like the Sun, the Moon, and the millions of stars in the sky.

items.stem: Briefly outline the problem-solving steps described for a pen that stops writing.
items.answer: If a pen stops writing, first guess the ink is finished and test by checking. If ink is present, guess it dried up and test differently.

items.stem: What are the three core actions of the scientific method after an observation and question?
items.answer: After observing and questioning, the core actions are: guess a possible (hypothesis), test this guess through experiments or observations, and analyze the results.

items.stem: Give an example from the chapter of someone applying scientific thinking in a daily task.
items.answer: An example is someone cooking who wonders why dal spilled from the cooker, questioning if too much water was used, thus applying scientific thinking.

items.stem: How does learning science, according to the chapter, improve our problem-solving abilities?
items.answer: Learning science develops our capabilities for finding solutions to bigger problems and solving more universal mysteries by understanding and applying the scientific method effectively.

items.stem: What does the chapter advise if you cannot find an answer to a question on your own?
items.answer: If you cannot find an alone, the chapter advises asking friends for help, as science is often a collaborative effort and discovery is more fun together.

items.stem: How is the journey of learning science portrayed in terms of duration in the chapter?
items.answer: The journey of learning science is portrayed as an ongoing exploration spanning several years, possibly extending beyond school, with continuous discoveries and new questions.

items.stem: What joyful activity is science compared to at the end of the chapter?
items.answer: At the end, science is compared to children joyfully enjoying the rain, emphasizing that science is fundamentally about joyful exploration and continuous wonder.

items.stem: What is the significance of being a “whys” person, as mentioned in the chapter’s conclusion?
items.answer: Being a “whys” person, someone who constantly asks ‘why’, is significant because this inquisitive nature is key to becoming a wise person through scientific exploration.

items.stem: What is the primary aim of the “Curiosity” textbook as suggested by the introductory chapter?
items.answer: The primary aim is to ignite students’ spirit of inquiry, encouraging them to explore their surroundings, ask questions, and understand the world using scientific principles.

items.stem: What examples of natural transformations does the chapter offer that can spark curiosity?
items.answer: The chapter offers transformations like a seed growing into a plant or a caterpillar changing into a beautiful butterfly as observations that can spark curiosity.

items.stem: The “Science” not just as a subject but as a “way of thinking.” Elaborate on this idea using details from the text, and explain why ‘Curiosity’ is deemed its most vital component.
items.answer: Science as a dynamic process of thinking, observing, and acting to comprehend our world and its mysteries. It’s an adventure of inquiry, not static knowledge. ‘Curiosity’ is vital because it’s the engine of this process. It’s the inherent urge to ask “why” and “how,” which fuels observation, questioning, exploration, and ultimately, the joy of discovery. The textbook itself is named “Curiosity” to emphasize its role in fostering this spirit, suggesting that true scientific engagement begins with a curious mind eager to explore and understand.

items.stem: Discuss the analogy “Science is like a giant and unending jigsaw puzzle”. How does this comparison explain the nature and progression of scientific knowledge?
items.answer: This analogy effectively portrays science as a vast, complex, and ever-expanding field of knowledge. Each new discovery is like adding a new piece to the puzzle, enhancing our understanding. The “unending” aspect highlights that science is never complete; each often uncovers more questions, leading to continuous investigation. It also implies that scientific knowledge is built progressively and collaboratively. Furthermore, the idea that pieces might be “put in the wrong place” reflects how scientific understanding can evolve, with new evidence correcting or refining previous theories and conclusions.

items.stem: “The most wonderful thing about science is that it is everywhere.” Justify this statement with at least four distinct examples provided in the chapter, covering different scales or environments.
items.answer: Science’s omnipresence with diverse examples. It’s in the vastness of outer space (stars shining), in natural processes (a flower blooming, a seed growing), in our homes (cooking in the kitchen, properties of water), and even in the materials we use daily (paper, plastic, metal). It ranges from studying microscopic grains of sand to massive mountains and from the depths of the ocean to our playgrounds. This pervasiveness shows that scientific principles and inquiry are applicable to understanding all aspects of our existence and environment, not just formal laboratory settings.

items.stem: Describe the scientific method using the everyday example of a pen that stops writing, as explained in the chapter. What are the general sequential steps involved in this method?
items.answer: When a pen stops writing, the scientific method begins with an observation and a question: “Why did it stop?” Then, a hypothesis is formed, e.g., “the ink finished.” This is tested by checking the refill. If the test fails (ink is present), a new hypothesis, like “the ink dried up,” is proposed and tested differently. The general steps are:

items.stem: How does the chapter encourage students to seek answers to their questions, and what role does collaboration play in the scientific process ?
items.answer: The chapter encourages students to pro-actively seek s by keenly observing, asking “how and why,” and applying the scientific method of guessing and testing. It stresses that this isn’t just for professional scientists. If an isn’t found individually, the text strongly advocates for collaboration, stating, “ask your friends to help you out!” It highlights that science is rarely a solitary pursuit; scientists worldwide work in teams, and discovering things together is portrayed as more effective and enjoyable, reflecting the collaborative nature of scientific advancement.

items.stem: What are some of the broad thematic areas of study hinted at in this introductory chapter that students will likely explore in the “Curiosity” textbook? Mention at least three.
items.answer: Firstly, students will explore Earth, its environment and the diversity of life, including how plants and animals grow. Secondly, they will delve into the science of everyday things, such as food, its composition, and different materials around us like paper, metal, and plastic. Thirdly, fundamental concepts like water and its properties, understanding temperature (hot and cold), and even extending curiosity to celestial bodies like the Sun, Moon, and stars will be part of their scientific journey.

items.stem: The scientific thinking is not confined to scientists alone but is applied in many daily life situations. Explain this with two distinct examples given in the text.
items.answer: A person cooking who wonders why dal spilled from the cooker, hypothesizing if there was too much water. This mirrors scientific questioning. Another example is a bicycle repair person trying to locate an air leak in a flat tyre, or an electrician determining why a bulb isn’t working by checking the bulb or switch. In both scenarios, individuals observe a problem, form a guess about the cause, and then investigate or test their guess, which is the essence of applying the scientific method in everyday problem-solving.

items.stem: Explain the chapter’s concluding message: “to be a wise person, you must be a ‘whys’ person!” What does this emphasize about learning and the scientific mindset?
items.answer: This concluding message powerfully emphasizes that wisdom is cultivated through persistent inquiry and a relentless desire to understand the underlying reasons for things – by constantly asking “why?” In the context of science, it reinforces that learning is an active process driven by curiosity, not passive memorization. Being a “whys” person signifies a commitment to questioning, investigating, and seeking explanations, which are the hallmarks of a scientific mindset. It suggests that true understanding and sagacity emerge from this inquisitive engagement with the world, promoting a lifelong habit of critical thinking and exploration.

items.stem: How does this first chapter aim to bridge the gap between students’ prior experiences in the Preparatory Stage and the formal introduction of Science in the Middle Stage?
items.answer: This chapter bridges the gap by acknowledging and validating students’ innate curiosity and exploratory experiences from the Preparatory Stage. It frames the formal introduction of Science in the Middle Stage not as a completely new or alien discipline, but as a continuation and enhancement of their natural desire to discover and understand. By emphasizing that science is an exciting journey fueled by asking questions— something children naturally do—it aims to make the transition smoother, fostering enthusiasm for the subject by connecting it to their inherent inquisitiveness.

items.stem: What perspective does the chapter offer regarding questions that might not be immediately answerable within Grade 6? How does it portray the nature of scientific learning over time?
items.answer: The chapter reassures students not to be disheartened if all their questions aren’t ed in Grade 6. It portrays scientific learning as a long-term, ongoing journey, stating they are “embarking upon a journey of science for the next five years or even beyond!” This perspective emphasizes that science is a process of continuous discovery rather than a collection of finite facts to be quickly memorized. It encourages sustained curiosity and patience, suggesting that deeper understanding unfolds progressively as they continue their exploration through their academic years and perhaps throughout their lives.

items.stem: Rohan observed that ice cubes melt faster when crushed into smaller pieces compared to a single large ice cube of the same total weight. He wondered why this happens, even though the amount of ice is the same. He thought it might have something to do with how much of the ice touches the warmer air. (i) What specific observation did Rohan make about melting ice? (ii) What was Rohan’s initial thought or hypothesis about why this occurs? (iii) Explain scientifically why crushed ice melts faster, relating to Rohan’s hypothesis. (iv) Suggest a simple way Rohan could visually compare the surface area of a whole ice cube versus crushed ice.
items.answer: (i) Rohan observed that crushed ice cubes melt faster than a single large ice cube of the same total weight. (ii) Rohan thought it might be related to how much of the ice surface is in contact with the warmer air. (iii) Crushing ice increases its total surface area exposed to the warmer surrounding air. More surface area means more contact points for heat transfer from the air to the ice, causing it to absorb heat and melt more quickly. (iv) Rohan could imagine dipping both in paint and then seeing how much area is painted; the crushed ice would show a much larger total painted area.

items.stem: During a school trip to a botanical garden, Priya noticed that some plants had labels indicating they “close their leaves at night.” That evening, she observed a plant in her own balcony whose leaves seemed to droop and fold inwards as it got dark. She wondered if this was a common behavior and why plants might do it. (i) What observation in the botanical garden and her balcony made Priya curious? (ii) What question did Priya’s observation lead her to ask? (iii) Suggest one possible reason why some plants might close their leaves at night. (iv) If Priya wanted to investigate further, what simple observation could she make over several days regarding her balcony plant and daylight?
items.answer: (i) Priya noticed plants that close their leaves at night in the garden and observed similar behavior in her balcony plant. (ii) Priya wondered if this leaf-closing behavior was common and why plants might do it. (iii) Closing leaves at night might help some plants conserve water by reducing surface area exposed to cooler night air, or it could be a way to protect against nocturnal herbivores or even conserve energy. (iv) Priya could observe her balcony plant at different times: sunrise, midday, sunset, and after dark for several days, noting the position of its leaves to see if there is a consistent pattern related to light.

items.stem: Ali was trying to dissolve sugar in three glasses of water: one with cold water, one with tap water (room temperature), and one with warm water. He used the same amount of sugar and water in each glass and stirred them equally. He noticed a difference in how quickly the sugar disappeared in each glass. (i) What was Ali trying to investigate with his three glasses of water and sugar? (ii) What difference did Ali likely observe regarding the sugar in the three glasses? (iii) Based on common scientific understanding, explain why this difference occurs. (iv) If Ali wanted to make his experiment more precise, what is one thing he should ensure is exactly the same for all three glasses, besides the amount of sugar and water?
items.answer: (i) Ali was trying to investigate how water temperature affects the speed at which sugar dissolves. (ii) Ali likely observed that the sugar dissolved fastest in the warm water, slower in the tap water, and slowest in the cold water. (iii) Sugar dissolves faster in warmer water because the water molecules have more energy and move more quickly, leading to more frequent collisions with sugar particles, breaking them apart and dispersing them faster. (iv) Ali should ensure that the stirring method (speed and duration) is exactly the same for all three glasses to ensure a fair comparison.

items.stem: While playing with a magnet, Sonia discovered that it attracted her steel hairpin but did not attract a copper coin or a plastic button. She tried it on various small objects around her house and started to group them based on whether they were attracted to the magnet or not. (i) What initial discovery did Sonia make with her magnet? (ii) What activity did Sonia engage in after her initial discovery? (iii) What property of materials was Sonia exploring through her activity? (iv) If Sonia found that an iron nail and a steel paperclip were attracted, but an aluminum foil piece was not, what could she conclude about aluminum compared to iron and steel?
items.answer: (i) Sonia discovered that her magnet attracted a steel hairpin but did not attract a copper coin or a plastic button. (ii) Sonia started testing the magnet on various small objects and began grouping them based on their attraction to the magnet. (iii) Sonia was exploring the magnetic property of materials, specifically identifying which materials are magnetic (attracted to a magnet) and which are non-magnetic. (iv) Sonia could conclude that aluminum is a non-magnetic material, unlike iron and steel, which are magnetic materials.

items.stem: A group of students was tasked with finding out how the length of a simple pendulum (a weight tied to a string) affects the time it takes to make one complete swing (its period). They made pendulums of different string lengths and timed 10 swings for each, then calculated the time for one swing. (i) What were the students investigating about a simple pendulum? (ii) What did they vary in their experiment, and what did they measure? (iii) Why was it a good idea for them to time 10 swings and then calculate the time for one swing, rather than just timing one swing? (iv) If they observed that longer pendulums took more time for one swing, what relationship would they be discovering?
items.answer: (i) The students were investigating how the length of a simple pendulum’s string affects the time it takes for one complete swing (its period). (ii) They varied the length of the pendulum string and measured the time taken for 10 swings (to then calculate the time for one swing). (iii) Timing 10 swings and then dividing by 10 reduces the impact of human reaction time errors in starting and stopping the timer, leading to a more accurate average time for a single swing. (iv) They would be discovering a direct relationship: as the length of the pendulum increases, the time period (time for one swing) also increases.
